cards.headline: Tiger Woods scheduled for change-of-plea hearing Wednesday in Martin County DUI case
cards.teaser: Tiger Woods is set to appear in Martin County court Wednesday for a plea conference in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods previously enter
cards.body:
Tiger Woods is set to appear in Martin County court Wednesday for a plea conference in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods previously entered a not guilty plea to misdemeanor charges of DUI with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test. Woods' attorney Douglas Duncan filed a notice Tuesday setting the hearing for 8:30 a.m.

 Wednesday before Judge Darren Steele at the Martin County Courthouse in Stuart. The filing lists the subject of the hearing as a Change of Plea.

 The charges stem from a March 27 crash on South Beach Road on Jupiter Island. Investigators said Woods attempted to pass a pickup truck towing a trailer, crossed double solid lines and struck the trailer, causing his Range Rover SUV to roll onto its side. Deputies who responded reported several signs of possible impairment, including bloodshot and glassy eyes, dilated pupils and slow, lethargic movements.

 They also found two pills later identified as hydrocodone in Woods' pocket. A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but authorities said he refused a urine test.

 Legal Analyst Robert Ellis told CBS12 News this change of plea could signal a deal has been reached between prosecutors and the defense. Ellis said prosecutors would consider the fact that Woods sought treatment almost immediately after his arrest, spending six weeks in a rehabilitation program in Switzerland. Woods told deputies he had been looking down at his phone and adjusting his radio before the crash.

 Woods' past could complicate negotiations. In 2017, he resolved a similar case in Palm Beach County through a diversion program that resulted in a reckless driving conviction, meaning that option is no longer available to him. Ellis said prosecutors could still negotiate a plea to reckless driving or another reduced charge, but Woods' prior history may factor into those discussions. The case has continued through the summer, including a judge's ruling allowing prosecutors access to Woods' medical records related to the case.
